title: URI Template
summary: A URI Template is a compact string describing a range of URIs through variable expansion. This RFC defines the syntax, the process for expanding a template into a URI reference, and guidelines for using templates on the Internet.

eli5.summary: A web address with blanks in it, like a form letter. Fill in the blanks and you get a real address.

questions: how to expand a uri template
what do the uri template operators mean
what is the explode modifier in uri templates
subtitle: A compact string with blanks in it that describes a whole family of URIs, and exactly how to fill the blanks in.

tldr.problem: Services often publish many similar URIs, such as one per user or one per search, and had no single agreed way to describe the pattern so that software could build the right URI from some values.
tldr.mechanism: A URI Template embeds expressions in braces, such as {term} or {?q,lang}. A template processor replaces each expression with the encoded values of its variables, following rules set by an optional operator and by Level 4 value modifiers.
tldr.outcome: Templates and the expansion rules are defined once, in four levels of increasing power, so different applications can share them. RFC 6570 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 6570 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of URI Templates. It builds on the URI syntax of RFC 3986.

sections.title: Describing a Space of URIs
sections.content:
A URI often names one resource inside a common pattern, for example http://example.com/~fred/ and http://example.com/~mark/. A URI Template is a compact sequence of characters that describes such a range of URIs through variable expansion. The first example above becomes http://example.com/~{username}/.

The RFC names three terms. An expression is the text between { and }, braces included. An expansion is the string you get after processing an expression. A template processor is a program or library that takes a template plus variable values and produces a URI reference.

Uses the RFC lists include discovery of available services, configuring resource mappings, defining computed links and specifying interfaces. A template may be absolute or relative, and it is expanded before any relative result is resolved to absolute form.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing a hundred nearly identical addresses, you write one with a gap in it. Anyone can fill the gap to get the address they need.

sections.title: Template Syntax
sections.content:
A template is a string of printable Unicode characters with zero or more embedded expressions, each delimited by a matching pair of braces. Characters outside expressions are literals: they are copied to the result if they are allowed in a URI, and otherwise copied as pct-encoded UTF-8 octets.

An expression is {, an optional operator, a comma-separated list of variable specifiers, and }. With no operator the expression is simple string expansion. The operators defined here are {+var}, {#var}, {.var}, {/var}, {;var}, {?var} and {&var}. The characters =, ,, !, @ and | are reserved for future extensions, and $, ( and ) are deliberately left unused so other tools can use them outside this specification.

Variable names are case-sensitive and may contain letters, digits, underscore, pct-encoded triplets and dots between name characters. A variable whose value is the empty string is defined; a variable that is unknown or set to something like null is undefined, and so is an empty list.

The grammar is written for Level 4. A processor limited to a lower level MAY skip the higher-level rules, but the RFC RECOMMENDS that all parsers implement the full syntax so unsupported levels can be reported properly.
sections.eli5: Anything in curly brackets is a blank to fill in. A little symbol right after the opening bracket tells the filler how to write the answer, like whether to start it with a question mark.

sections.title: Four Levels and Value Modifiers
sections.content:
The RFC describes templates in four gradual levels, because most earlier processors only implemented the default expression type.

  • Level 1: simple string expansion, one variable per expression, such as {var}.
  • Level 2: adds the plus operator, as in {+var}, for values that may contain reserved URI characters, and the crosshatch, as in {#var}, for fragment identifiers.
  • Level 3: allows several comma-separated variables per expression and adds the dot, slash, semicolon, question mark and ampersand operators.
  • Level 4: adds value modifiers on each variable.

The prefix modifier (a colon and a length, as in {var:3}) limits the expansion to the first characters of the value. The length is a positive integer below 10000, counted in characters rather than octets so a multi-octet character or pct-encoded triplet is never split. With var set to value, {var:3} gives val, and {var:30} gives value. Prefix modifiers do not apply to composite values.

The explode modifier (an asterisk, as in {list*}) treats a variable as a list or as an associative array of name and value pairs, and expands each member as if it were a separate variable. For example, find{?year*} with three years gives find?year=1965&year=2000&year=2012.
sections.eli5: Level 1 is a single blank. Higher levels let you fill several blanks at once, cut a word short, or spill a whole list into the address one item at a time.

sections.title: How Expansion Works
sections.content:
Expansion scans the template from start to end, copying literals and replacing each expression with the result of applying its operator to each named variable. Each variable's value MUST be formed before expansion starts, and a variable used more than once MUST keep the same value throughout. Expressions cannot be nested.

Undefined variables are ignored. If every variable in an expression is undefined, the expansion is the empty string, so with both query and number undefined, http://www.example.com/foo{?query,number} expands to http://www.example.com/foo.

What may pass through unencoded depends on the operator. Reserved ({+var}) and fragment ({#var}) expansion allow unreserved characters, reserved characters and pct-encoded triplets. All other types allow only unreserved characters, so a % in a value MUST become %25. Non-ASCII text is first encoded as UTF-8 and then pct-encoded octet by octet. A user-supplied value SHOULD be normalized as Unicode Normalization Form C first.

Each operator has its own prefix and separator, shown in the diagram. The ; operator drops the = for an empty value, while ? and & keep it. For example, with x as 1024, y as 768 and empty as an empty string, {;x,y,empty} gives ;x=1024;y=768;empty and {?x,y,empty} gives ?x=1024&y=768&empty=.
sections.eli5: The filler walks along the address, copying plain parts and swapping each blank for its answer. If there is no answer, the blank just disappears. Odd characters are written in a safe code so the address does not break.

sections.title: Operators in Practice
sections.content:
The RFC gives worked examples for every operator. With who as fred, list as red, green and blue, and path as /foo/bar:

  • {who} gives fred, and {hello} with Hello World! gives Hello%20World%21.
  • {+path}/here gives /foo/bar/here, keeping the slashes.
  • {#var} gives #value.
  • X{.var} gives X.value.
  • {/list*} gives /red/green/blue.
  • {;who} gives ;who=fred.
  • ?fixed=yes{&x} gives ?fixed=yes&x=1024.

A slash inside a value is pct-encoded by operators other than plus and crosshatch, so {/who,dub} with dub set to me/too gives /fred/me%2Ftoo. Composite values show the difference exploding makes: {?keys} gives ?keys=semi,%3B,dot,.,comma,%2C, while {?keys*} gives ?semi=%3B&dot=.&comma=%2C.
sections.eli5: The same list of colors can be written as one comma-joined string or as separate repeated items, depending on whether you add a star. The little symbol decides whether it starts with a slash, a question mark or a dot.

sections.title: Errors and Limitations
sections.content:
If a character outside an expression does not match the grammar, processing SHOULD stop. The result SHOULD contain the expanded part followed by the unexpanded remainder, and the location and type of error SHOULD be reported to the calling application. If the problem is inside an expression, such as an unrecognized operator or modifier, the unprocessed part of the expression SHOULD be copied unexpanded, processing SHOULD continue, and the error SHOULD be reported. A result from an error might not be a valid URI reference and is only meant for diagnostics.

The RFC states some limits plainly. A template describes a superset of identifiers, so not every expansion matches a real resource. URI Templates are not URIs: they should not be used where a URI is expected unless a processor expands them first, and distinct field or attribute names should be used to tell the two apart. Running a template in reverse to extract variables only works well when expressions are delimited by the start or end of the URI or by characters that cannot appear in an expansion, and regular expression languages are generally better for that job.
sections.eli5: If part of the form letter is garbled, the filler keeps what it could do, leaves the broken bit as it was, and tells you where the problem was. A form letter is also not a real address until it has been filled in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A URI Template contains no active or executable content. The risk is that an attacker given control of the template, or of values in an expression that allows reserved characters, might craft unanticipated URIs. The RFC says the concern depends on who supplies the template, who supplies the values, whether expansion runs on client or server, and where the resulting URIs are used.

In server frameworks, templates guide where data may appear in later requests, so the concern is how the server handles user-provided data. In client-side use, a template behaves much like an HTML form. Care ought to be taken that dangerous strings, such as those beginning with javascript:, do not appear in an expansion unless both the template and the values come from a trusted source. Other considerations are the same as for URIs in RFC 3986.
sections.eli5: If a stranger gets to write the blanks or the answers, they might sneak in a bad address. So only fill in blanks with things from people you trust.
